strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored gap: whether machine learning Hamiltonians (MLHs) are competitive as direct energy-force predictors rather than just reconstruction models or SCF accelerators, backed by a well-motivated benchmark that computes energies and forces directly from predicted Hamiltonians using a consistent PySCF-based pipeline.

Strong and consistent empirical improvements: QHFlow2 reduces Hamiltonian error by 40-50% with fewer parameters, achieves up to 20x lower energy MAE than MLIP baselines on MD17/rMD17 and QH9, and is the first Hamiltonian predictor to approach NequIP-level force accuracy.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of individual design choices: the two-stage SO(2)/SO(3) pair update (Table 10), flow matching vs. regression (Table 11), initial Hamiltonian usage (Tables 12-13), and the readout tensor-expansion degree (Table 14), providing good evidence that the architectural choices are responsible for gains rather than confounds.

Extensive supplementary analysis strengthens the soundness of claims: a perturbative argument and empirical scaling-law verification for why energy errors shrink faster than force errors, finite-difference vs analytic force consistency checks, MO-basis block error decomposition explaining why global Hamiltonian MAE doesn't fully predict downstream accuracy, geometry optimization and Hessian/PES fidelity comparisons, zero-shot generalization to much larger molecules, and reactive-site (FMO) robustness tests.

Reasonable attention to reproducibility: detailed hyperparameter tables, training/architecture specifications for all model sizes and baselines, dataset construction/splits described, and stated intent to release code and the recomputed rMD17 benchmark.

Reports favorable and consistent scaling behavior with both model capacity and training data, and documents practical runtime/memory trade-offs (inference speed, SCF-acceleration speedups) relevant for real-world adoption.
weaknesses: Several key comparisons are not fully controlled: on QH9, MLIP baselines (MACE, Equiformer, EquiformerV2) are taken from published QM9 results rather than retrained on the same QH9 splits/training set sizes used for QHFlow2, which may bias the reported 20x energy-error reduction; similarly, HELM and QHNetV2 comparisons rely on numbers from papers with unavailable codebases rather than fully controlled reproduction.

The architecture is primarily a recombination of existing components (eSEN's SO(2) backbone, QHNet's tensor-expansion readout and non-diagonal pair update, and Kim et al.'s flow-matching training), so the technical novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior MLH work, even though the empirical execution and combination are effective.

Forces derived from the predicted Hamiltonian are one-shot and not guaranteed to be strictly conservative (as the authors acknowledge), and end-to-end downstream evaluation cost is dominated by the DFT/Fock-build post-processing step rather than the network itself, which could limit practical throughput compared to MLIPs despite the reported speed/memory tables.

The method is restricted to fixed functional/basis and restricted closed-shell systems; spin-resolved/open-shell extension and cross-functional transfer are left as future work, narrowing the immediate scope of applicability.

Some claims (e.g., 'first Hamiltonian model to reach NequIP-level force accuracy') are based on average force MAE across six molecules that is close but only marginally better/comparable (1.00 vs 0.93 in the linear-scale panel), and the significance of this near-parity versus true state-of-the-art MLIPs (e.g., MACE-level accuracy) is not deeply interrogated.

The manuscript is very dense with a large appendix (36 pages) containing numerous additional analyses; while thorough, this raises concerns about whether all claims in the main text are fully self-contained and digestible without heavy reliance on supplementary material, which could affect clarity for readers evaluating the core claims.

strengths: The paper introduces a genuinely useful benchmarking framework that evaluates Hamiltonian predictors via directly computed downstream energies and forces (rather than reconstruction-only metrics), which addresses a real gap noted in prior literature (e.g., Kaniselvan et al. 2025).

Extensive and largely controlled experiments on the MD17/rMD17 benchmark, where MLIP baselines and Hamiltonian predictors are retrained under identical splits and evaluation pipelines, giving credible apples-to-apples comparisons for that portion of the study.

Thorough ablation studies (two-stage pair update, flow-matching vs. regression, initialization strategy, readout angular degree, density-matrix vs. Hamiltonian prediction) that support specific architectural design choices.

Useful supplementary analyses (perturbative energy-force error scaling argument, MO-basis block-wise error decomposition explaining the vv/oo error asymmetry, Hessian/PES fidelity, geometry optimization tests) that provide physical insight beyond simple MAE tables and partially validate the practical utility of the predicted forces.

Reasonably detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters, dataset splits, training configurations) and an explicit, honest limitations section covering functional/basis-set specificity, closed-shell restriction, and non-conservative one-shot forces.
weaknesses: The headline QH9 comparisons (e.g., '20× lower energy error than MACE') are not controlled: MLIP numbers are taken from published QM9 papers using different splits and larger training sets than the QH9-stable-id split QHFlow2 is trained/evaluated on, as the paper itself acknowledges. This substantially weakens the central quantitative claims presented prominently in the abstract and title.

Forces are computed as one-shot analytic gradients from non-self-consistent densities induced by the predicted Hamiltonian, and the paper acknowledges these are not guaranteed to be conservative. This is a serious caveat for the framing of the model as suitable for 'practical atomistic simulations' (e.g., MD), since non-conservative forces can cause energy drift; the abstract does not sufficiently flag this limitation upfront.

The computational cost of the proposed evaluation pipeline is large: Table 18 shows the total per-structure runtime for QHFlow2 (~1.5s, dominated by the PySCF Fock-build/energy-force evaluation) is roughly an order of magnitude slower than direct MLIP inference (~0.1–0.2s). This practical overhead is a major consideration for real deployment but is understated relative to the accuracy-focused abstract claims.

Generalization breaks down at larger molecular scales: the zero-shot PubChemQH evaluation (Section G.7) shows the SCF cycle ratio exceeding 100% for 80–98 atom molecules, meaning the predicted Hamiltonian actually slows down convergence rather than helping, and per-atom energy MAE exceeds 1 eV/atom in that regime — undermining claims of robust practical utility beyond the training distribution.

The headline comparison target (NequIP) for 'first Hamiltonian model to reach MLIP-level force accuracy' is a relatively dated MLIP baseline; a more contemporary comparison (eSEN, included only in the appendix) shows a more mixed picture, suggesting the main-text framing may be somewhat selectively favorable.

QH9-dynamic-mol results (unseen-molecule generalization) remain substantially worse than stable-id/ood and dynamic-geo splits, indicating that generalization to genuinely novel molecules is still a weak point not sufficiently emphasized in the main narrative.

The model requires retraining for each fixed DFT functional/basis set and is restricted to closed-shell RKS systems, limiting immediate applicability across the diversity of quantum chemistry use cases claimed by the broader motivation.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and clearly needed benchmark that directly evaluates energies and forces computed from predicted Hamiltonians, addressing a real gap identified by prior work (Kaniselvan et al., 2025) between reconstruction-based and downstream evaluation of MLH models.

QHFlow2 architecture is a principled combination of an eSEN-style SO(2)-equivariant backbone with a novel two-stage (SO(2) initialization + SO(3) tensor-product refinement) pair update, and the ablations (Table 10) convincingly show the refinement stage improves off-diagonal accuracy and robustness to cutoff/radial-basis choices.

Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple benchmarks (MD17, rMD17, QH9, plus ∇2DFT and PubChemQH generalization tests), with substantial reductions in Hamiltonian error (40-50%) using fewer parameters and faster inference than prior MLH baselines.

Exceptionally thorough supplementary analysis (Appendix G) that goes beyond typical benchmarking: a perturbative argument and empirical verification for why energy errors scale quadratically while force errors scale linearly with Hamiltonian error, finite-difference vs analytic force comparisons, MO-basis block-wise error decomposition explaining why global Hamiltonian MAE doesn't predict downstream energy accuracy, geometry optimization and Hessian/PES fidelity studies, and zero-shot extrapolation to much larger molecules and to reactive bond-stretching scenarios.
Careful scaling studies (data and model size) and a runtime/memory analysis showing favorable trade-offs relative to prior Hamiltonian predictors.
Honest and detailed limitations section acknowledging fixed functional/basis restriction, closed-shell-only scope, non-conservative one-shot forces, and end-to-end cost dominated by DFT evaluation.
Reasonably reproducible: detailed hyperparameters, architecture tables, dataset statistics, and environment specifications are provided for both QHFlow2 and baselines.
weaknesses: The comparison against MLIP baselines on QH9 (Figure 3) relies on published QM9 results as reference points rather than retraining MLIPs under identical splits/settings as QHFlow2, which weakens the fairness/comparability of the headline '20x lower energy error' and '92-95% relative error reduction' claims for that dataset.

The paper's framing (title and abstract) emphasizes that QHFlow2 achieves 'NequIP-level' force accuracy and is an 'accurate energy-force predictor,' but Table 18 shows the end-to-end evaluation cost (Hamiltonian inference + PySCF energy/force computation) is roughly 10-20x slower than direct MLIP evaluation, a practical limitation that is understated relative to the strength of the framing.

The theoretical/empirical analysis in Section G.8 itself shows force errors scale only linearly (not quadratically, as energy errors do) with Hamiltonian error, implying forces remain intrinsically harder to make highly accurate via this pipeline; this tension between the strong marketing claims and the paper's own mechanistic explanation could be discussed more prominently in the main text.

One-shot analytic forces from non-self-consistent densities are not guaranteed conservative, which is a nontrivial concern for downstream MD applications (acknowledged but not empirically stress-tested with long MD trajectories/energy conservation experiments).

Restriction to restricted closed-shell systems and a fixed DFT functional/basis limits immediate applicability to more general chemistry (open-shell systems, multiple functionals), and no experiments at OMol25 scale are provided, leaving open how well the approach scales to more diverse, larger real-world datasets.
